strengths: Comprehensive and rigorous experimental design covering 14 explanation methods, 4 models, 2 datasets, 3 bias types, and 6 fairness metrics
Clear and nuanced findings, particularly the important distinction that explanations work well for bias detection but fail for model selection
Excellent reproducibility with detailed implementation details, code promises, and extensive appendices
Addresses timely and practically important problem of bridging explainability and fairness
Demonstrates that explanation-based bias detection remains effective in debiased models and outperforms LLM judgments
Systematic evaluation across both encoder-only and decoder-only models showing generality across model types
weaknesses: Limited generalization: study confined to hate speech detection task only; results may not transfer to other fairness-critical NLP tasks like coreference or occupation classification
Incomplete theoretical explanation for why explanations fail for model selection (RQ2) while succeeding for bias detection (RQ1); proposed mechanism is speculative and not directly tested
Critical finding buried in footnote 2: group fairness metrics show no correlation with explanations, which significantly limits applicability but is not prominently discussed
No correction for multiple comparisons (~100+ statistical tests across 14 methods × 3 biases × multiple settings); confidence intervals not provided for correlation coefficients

Methodological choices inadequately justified: (1) sensitive token vocabulary not validated through ablation, (2) use of maximum reliance score arbitrary when multiple sensitive tokens present, (3) hyperparameter tuning strategy differs from prior work without clear justification, (4) test set sampling strategy may not reflect real-world distributions
Limited theoretical understanding of why certain methods (L2-based, Occlusion) outperform others; claim that mean-based methods fail due to direction determination lacks rigorous validation
LLM comparison limited to single model (Qwen3) with potentially constraining prompt; Grad L2 Binary baseline appears cherry-picked
No human evaluation of whether practitioners actually find explanations useful for fairness decisions, limiting practical impact assessment
Dataset construction (excluding slurs) may introduce selection bias favoring explanations; potential filtering effects not discussed
Key results relegated to appendices (Jigsaw results mostly in Appendix B-E); important limitations (group fairness) not highlighted in main text

strengths: Comprehensive empirical study: First large-scale quantitative analysis of explainability-fairness relationship in NLP, examining 14 explanation methods across multiple datasets, model types, and bias types
Clear actionable findings: Specific conclusions about which explanation methods work for which purposes (Occlusion and L2-based methods effective for bias detection but not model selection)
Appropriate methodology: Use of both group and individual fairness metrics provides complete picture; inclusion of both encoder and decoder-only models reflects modern NLP landscape
Robustness analysis: Investigation of bias detection in explanation-debiased models (Section 5) is valuable, showing certain explanations remain effective even after debiasing interventions
Good reproducibility: Comprehensive implementation details and commitment to open-source code; extensive appendices with full results
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: Applies existing explanation methods to existing task without proposing new methods or theoretical insights; more an engineering study than scientific contribution

Questionable practical significance: RQ1's finding that explanations correlate with individual unfairness offers limited value if practitioners can directly compute fairness metrics on validation data. RQ2 findings are nearly trivial—unsurprising that direct fairness measurements outperform indirect proxies. RQ3 improvements are modest and inconsistent

Narrow scope and generalization concerns: Restricted to hate speech detection with only three bias types and binary/ternary groups; artificial dataset construction via identity-term filtering; 2,000-8,000 training examples per type; findings unlikely to transfer to other NLP tasks or subtle biases

Incomplete analysis: No computational cost comparison despite noting explanations are expensive; missing intuitive explanations for why Occlusion vastly outperforms gradient methods; fairness-accuracy tradeoffs not systematically analyzed; results highly inconsistent across metrics suggesting fundamental challenges not discussed

Weak experimental choices: Model selection in RQ1 uses unjustified criterion ('highest average Avgiu') potentially biasing results; RQ2 uses fairness-balanced hyperparameter tuning possibly biasing toward explanation-based methods; LLM comparison uses overly simple baselines

Statistical rigor gaps: Most results lack error bars/confidence intervals; no multiple-comparison correction despite 14 methods; why faithfulness doesn't predict bias detection ability (Section G) deserves deeper investigation but remains superficial
Limited use case articulation: Paper doesn't convincingly explain when practitioners would use explanations instead of computing fairness directly, undermining practical motivation for the work

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation—first large-scale quantitative analysis of explainability-fairness relationship with 14 explanation methods, 4 models, 2 datasets, and 3 bias types
Important nuanced findings: positive results for bias detection (RQ1) and bias mitigation (RQ3), but importantly negative finding for model selection (RQ2) that challenges assumptions
Strong experimental methodology with multiple fairness metrics (group and individual), statistical significance testing, and well-motivated design choices
Practical value with clear actionable recommendations for practitioners on which explanation methods work best for different purposes
Robustness analysis showing explanation-based bias detection remains effective even in explanation-debiased models is a valuable contribution
Clear presentation with good visualizations and well-structured research questions that address complementary aspects of the problem
weaknesses: Limited scope: exclusive focus on hate speech detection with only English-language data limits generalizability; findings may not transfer to other fairness-sensitive NLP tasks

Insufficient analysis of RQ2 failure: explanation for why explanations fail at model selection is superficial; missing ablations on validation set size and systematic exploration of alternative approaches

Limited methodological novelty: primarily empirical evaluation of existing methods rather than proposing new explanation or debiasing approaches; bias mitigation uses standard regularization from prior work

Incomplete investigation of key findings: important result that faithfulness doesn't predict bias detection ability (Appendix G) relegated to appendix; limited analysis of explanation method differences and dataset variations
Statistical concerns: only 3 validation set selections for decoder-only models is quite small; some results lack error bars; potential multiple testing without correction mentioned

Underdeveloped theoretical insights: paper remains largely empirical without mechanistic understanding of why explanations work for detection but not model selection, or what properties enable bias detection

strengths: First comprehensive quantitative study bridging explainability and fairness in NLP hate speech detection, addressing an important gap
Extensive experimental design with 16 explanation methods, multiple models (BERT, RoBERTa, Llama, Qwen), two datasets, and three bias types
Systematic methodology addressing three well-motivated research questions with clear experimental protocols
Provides actionable practical guidance: specific recommendation of Occlusion/L2 methods for bias detection and strong evidence against using explanations for model selection
Thorough supplementary analyses including human studies, faithfulness analysis, and robustness checks in debiased models
Strong reproducibility with detailed implementation details and promised code release
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: findings are largely confirmatory (RQ1 and RQ3 expected; RQ2 negative result somewhat unsurprising)
Narrow scope limited to hate speech detection with only minimal generalization validation (sentiment analysis in Appendix); unclear how findings transfer to other tasks and domains
Simplistic bias representation using pre-defined sensitive token vocabularies that miss subtle, contextual bias; reduced vocabulary degradation suggests this is a significant limitation
Insufficient analysis of underlying mechanisms: why do L2/Occlusion methods work better? Why doesn't faithfulness predict bias detection ability?
RQ2 analysis potentially unfair: comparing indirect explanation signals to direct fairness evaluation; alternative formulations and metrics not explored
Methodological choices are simplifications: max absolute value aggregation for multiple sensitive tokens, individual fairness focus over group fairness, exclusion of slur-based examples may ease task

strengths: Comprehensive empirical study spanning multiple dimensions: 16 explanation methods, diverse model architectures (BERT, RoBERTa, Llama, Qwen), two datasets, and multiple debiasing approaches with extensive ablations
Honest and nuanced findings documenting mixed results without cherry-picking, including the interesting negative result that explanations fail for model selection (RQ2)
Important and timely research question addressing the relationship between explainability and fairness, which is increasingly critical for NLP systems
Strong empirical rigor demonstrated through multiple datasets, consistent findings across model types, statistical significance testing, and careful experimental design
Practical actionable guidance identifying which explanation methods (Occlusion, L2-based) work effectively for bias detection and which work for training-time mitigation
Extensive supplementary materials with generalization tests, human studies, faithfulness analysis, and reproducibility details enhancing confidence in results
weaknesses: Limited novelty as primarily a validation study of existing ideas: no new explanation methods, debiasing techniques, or fairness metrics proposed; the work essentially asks 'do existing approaches work?' rather than advancing the field

Weak analysis of the most interesting finding (RQ2 failure): vague explanation that 'debiasing alters behaviors' without investigating why validation-set fairness so thoroughly outperforms explanation-based methods or what fundamental limitations exist

Shallow mechanistic understanding: the paper documents what works empirically but lacks analysis of why Occlusion/L2-based methods succeed, why faithfulness doesn't correlate with fairness-correlation (Appendix I), or why mean vs. L2-based approaches differ so dramatically

Paradoxically narrow scope despite comprehensiveness: single primary task (hate speech detection), heavy focus on individual fairness over standard group fairness, only 3 bias types, and limited cross-task validation (only 1000 sentiment examples)

RQ3 results appear modest and lack rigorous evaluation: no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals for improvements, unclear fairness-accuracy tradeoffs masked by harmonic mean reporting, and absence of simpler baseline comparisons (e.g., removing sensitive features)

Methodological concerns with arbitrary design choices: max absolute attribution for multiple tokens lacks justification, individual unfairness metric design underexplored, hyperparameter tuning on fairness-balanced metric raises realism questions

Presentation issues with critical analyses relegated to appendices: RQ2 failure and faithfulness-fairness disconnect deserve main-text investigation; 16 methods × 3 RQs creates overwhelming result tables without adequate synthesis
Human study (Appendix J) is small-scale (48 examples) with artificial annotation design (either directed or undirected) and mixed/inconclusive results providing limited impact
Overstated generalization claims: Appendix H generalization tests use only 1000 examples with single bias type, insufficient to support broad transferability claims
Insufficient engagement with why explanations fail for model selection, representing a key theoretical gap that deserves deeper investigation but receives only cursory treatment

strengths: First large-scale quantitative study of explainability-fairness intersection in NLP, filling an important gap in the literature
Exceptionally comprehensive experimental design spanning 16 explanation methods, multiple model architectures, datasets, bias types, and fairness metrics
Important and actionable findings, especially RQ2's negative result that explanations cannot reliably select fair models, which challenges field assumptions
Thorough robustness analysis including debiased models, comparison with LLM-as-a-judge, human studies, and generalization tests across tasks and model types
Clear identification of which explanation methods work best (Occlusion, L2-based methods) with practical recommendations for practitioners
Excellent reproducibility with detailed implementation details, promised code release, and comprehensive documentation
Well-written and well-organized paper with clear research questions and sophisticated understanding of the complexity of fairness-explainability relationships
Addresses important concerns such as whether explanation-debiased models can mask bias, providing evidence they remain detectable with certain methods
weaknesses: Limited primary scope: focus on hate speech detection as sole application domain, with only preliminary generalization to sentiment analysis; broader scope across tasks would strengthen impact

RQ2 negative result, while important, somewhat expected—the conclusion that direct fairness computation outperforms explanation-based metrics is intuitive; deeper analysis of why model selection fails would be valuable
Group fairness metrics computed but under-analyzed relative to individual fairness; for a fairness-focused paper, more thorough group fairness investigation would be valuable
Requires manual definition of sensitive tokens in advance; while robustness to incomplete vocabulary shown, no systematic approach to discovering sensitive tokens is proposed
Statistical rigor could be stronger: no confidence intervals reported, no correction for multiple comparisons despite numerous tests, informal significance assessment
Fairness-balanced metric for hyperparameter tuning differs from prior work (Dimanov et al.), making direct comparison less clean; ablation on this choice would strengthen results
No clear single recommendation across all RQs and tasks; while honest about complexity, practical guidance for practitioners is somewhat limited
LLM-as-a-judge evaluation limited to race bias subset with only two LLMs; more comprehensive evaluation would strengthen claims
Some figures (especially 7-10) are crowded with many methods and difficult to parse; visualization could be improved
Missing deeper analysis of fairness-accuracy trade-offs and why certain explanation methods excel at specific tasks
